A .jot is plain text, but the tasks, events and numbers in it can be read by a program. This guide covers what you can do with them: put your events on your calendar, bring in numbers from a fitness app, carry unfinished tasks forward, and connect to other services.

What gets sent, and when. Nothing in Jot reaches the internet unless you run something that says it will, or turn on a setting that says it will. Calendar, CSV and journal-writing tools work locally. Spotify sign-in and playback fetches contact Spotify only when chosen. Service results become ordinary Jot: structured import records or a readable listening note. Your journal text is not sent to Spotify, and the .jot file stays the master copy.

In the workspace: the Tools row

Above the writing, in Write:

Commands (Ctrl+K / Cmd+K) searches these tools together with formatting, find/replace, the outline and editable entry templates. On mobile, use All tools to expand the secondary buttons. Each template is reviewed before insertion; its prompts stay blank until you fill them in. Writing tools, templates, suggestions and search run locally.

Tool What it does
Music & background media adds a plain-text music note, optionally filled from Spotify after sign-in and review
Today ＋ adds today's dated entry, if there is none, and puts the cursor in it. "Today" follows My day starts at in Preferences (midnight unless you change it), as Carry tasks forward and Week review do
Carry tasks forward → open tasks from earlier days are marked [>] (moved) where they were, and written again under today
Week review adds a review of this week: how many tasks were done, which are still open, each number's average, a chart and two questions
Calendar .ics ↓ your events and dated tasks as a calendar file: import it into Google Calendar, Apple Calendar, Outlook …
Numbers .csv ↓ · Tasks .csv ↓ the numbers (date, metric, value, unit) or the tasks, for a spreadsheet
Import numbers ↥ numbers from a CSV (a health or fitness app's export) written into their days

A tool that changes your writing does it in one step, so Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac) takes it back.

Events and tasks on your calendar

The calendar file has:

  • Events (lines starting o ). If the line has a time (19:00, 7:30pm, at 21) the event is an hour long at that time; otherwise it lasts all day. A bare "at 7" is not a time: morning or evening? Write 7pm or 19:00.
  • Tasks that are open ([ ], [!]) on a dated day, as to-dos due that day. Done, moved and cancelled tasks are left out.
### 2026-10-28 | Wednesday

o Dentist 09:30
o Market, all day
[ ] Post the letter

Each event and task keeps the same identity in every export, so importing a newer file updates entries instead of adding them twice. Google Calendar shows events but not to-dos: in VS Code, turn on jot.automation.calendar.tasksAsEvents to put tasks in as all-day events too.

Numbers from a fitness or health app

Most apps (Google Fit, Garmin, Fitbit, sleep and step counters, a spreadsheet) can export a CSV. Jot needs one column of dates and columns of numbers; the column names become the metrics, and a unit in brackets is kept (Sleep (h) becomes metric sleep, unit h):

Date,Steps,Sleep (h)
2026-10-26,8200,7.5
2026-10-27,6400,6.75
  • Each number goes into its day. If your template has an empty value: for that metric on that day, it is filled in where it is; otherwise the number is added at the end of the day as a measurement, with source: naming the file.
  • A day that already has that number is left alone, so importing the same file twice adds nothing.
  • Several rows on one day (steps by the hour) are added up in the workspace. On the command line or in VS Code you can choose to average them instead (heart rate), or keep the last.
  • Dates like 2026-10-26, 2026/10/26 and 2026-10-26 07:30 always work. A date like 03/04/2026 could be either way round, so it is left out and counted; on the command line, --day-first reads it as the 3rd of April.

The numbers then chart like any others: see Numbers and charts.

Health data

Import health data in the Tools row reads a health app's own export and writes one number per day for each kind you choose. It works on this device: nothing is uploaded, no account is needed, and nothing changes until you press Add to journal (Ctrl+Z takes it out again).

  • Apple Health: in the Health app, tap your picture, then Export All Health Data. Unzip export.zip and choose apple_health_export/export.xml. The file can be very large; it is read in pieces, up to 2 GB.
  • Health Connect, Google Fit, Fitbit, Garmin, Oura: choose the daily CSV the app (or an export app) writes. Known columns are read with their units; others are listed as left out. A CSV Jot doesn't recognise is read like any other numbers CSV, still without the columns listed under "Never read" below.

You then tick the numbers you want and choose the dates (the last 30 days to begin with); the dialog shows how many days each has and every record it will add or fill. How a day's readings become one number:

Number Metric A day's number
Steps, distance, active energy, flights, exercise minutes steps, distance, active-energy, flights, exercise the day's total. When two devices count the same day (a phone and a watch), the larger total is used, not both added
Heart rate, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, blood oxygen, respiratory rate heart-rate, resting-heart-rate, hrv, spo2, respiratory-rate the day's average. The lowest and highest (heart-rate-min, heart-rate-max …) are there to tick if you want them
Sleep sleep (h) hours asleep (not in bed, not awake), every source merged so overlapping apps count once, given to the date you woke up. A nap counts on the day it ends
Body mass, body fat body-mass, body-fat the last reading of the day
Mindful minutes mindful (min) the day's total, overlapping sessions counted once

A reading belongs to the day written in the export, in the time zone it was recorded in. Units stay as the app wrote them (kg or lb, km or mi); a metric recorded in two units becomes two metrics (body-mass-kg, body-mass-lb) rather than being converted, and sleep a CSV counts in minutes or seconds is sleep-minutes or sleep-seconds, so it never shares an axis with hours. A template blank whose unit: differs from the number's is left empty and counted. The one change is blood oxygen and body fat, which Apple writes as fractions (0.97) and Jot as the percent they mean (97 %). Each record says how its day was counted and where it came from:

### 2026-10-26 | Monday

:::record measurement #sleep-2026-10-26
metric: sleep
value: 7.25
unit: h
aggregation: sum
source: Apple Health export.xml
:::

Never read, whatever the file holds: medications, lab results and clinical records (including export_cda.xml), reproductive and sexual health, and location (workout routes, latitude and longitude columns). They stay in the export, out of a journal you may share, sync or print. Readiness, sleep and stress scores are an app's calculations rather than measurements, so they are left out too, and Jot never turns any number into a statement about your health.

On the command line, jot import-health export.xml --list shows what a file holds; then, for example, jot import-health export.xml --into journal.jot --metric steps --metric sleep --since 2026-10-01 --dry-run.

The jot command line

cli/jot.mjs in the Jot project (Node 20 or later) does the same things from a terminal, so scripts, scheduled jobs and Apple Shortcuts can use them:

jot tasks journal.jot --status open          # today's to-do list, anywhere
jot events journal.jot --since 2026-10-01
jot numbers journal.jot                      # CSV
jot ics journal.jot -o ~/Calendars/jot.ics   # a calendar file
jot import fit.csv --into journal.jot        # numbers in, into their days
jot import-health export.xml --into journal.jot --metric steps --since 2026-10-01
jot today journal.jot                        # today's entry
jot rollover journal.jot                     # carry open tasks to today
jot review journal.jot                       # this week's review
jot json journal.jot                         # everything, as JSON
jot query journal.jot                        # the answers to the query records in it
jot query journal.jot --show tasks --tag health --period week   # or ask one here

The reading commands never change a file. The writing commands say what they changed, and --dry-run prints the result instead of saving it. jot help lists every option.

Locking a journal with a passphrase

jot lock journal.jot --recovery-code         # makes journal.jotlock; asks for the passphrase twice, shows a recovery code once
jot unlock journal.jotlock -o copy.jot       # the journal back, exactly as it was
jot unlock journal.jotlock --recovery        # ...with the recovery code instead
jot lock-info journal.jotlock                # its ways in

A locked journal is encrypted with your passphrase (AES-256-GCM, with the key made from the passphrase by PBKDF2), using only what is built into Node and browsers. Anyone with the passphrase can open it, with Jot or with a few lines of Python or Node (the Jot Lock recipes); nobody else can.

  • Nobody can reset it. Jot never keeps or sends your passphrase or recovery code. Without one of them, the journal cannot be opened by anyone, you included. Keep them in a password manager.
  • Passkeys and security keys added in the workspace work only there, on the site they were added on; from the command line, use the passphrase or the recovery code.
  • Locking makes a copy. The unlocked journal is still there until you delete it, and a deleted file can stay on a disk.
  • It hides the writing, not the file: its name, size and dates still show, so give it a neutral name. It does not help if someone uses your unlocked computer, or makes you give up the passphrase.
  • For scripts, the passphrase can come from JOT_PASSPHRASE; it is never taken as an argument, where other programs could see it.

The workspace opens and saves locked journals too: see Locking a journal.

In VS Code

The Jot extension has the same commands (press Ctrl+Shift+P and type "Jot"): Today's Entry (Ctrl+Alt+T), Carry Open Tasks to Today, Add a Week Review, Export Calendar (.ics), Export as CSV and Import Numbers from CSV. Each change is one edit, so Undo takes it back.

To keep your calendar up to date without thinking about it, set jot.automation.exportOnSave.ics to a file in a folder that syncs (iCloud Drive, Dropbox, Google Drive, a web folder). Every time you save, the calendar file is written again, and a calendar app that subscribes to that file sees your journal's events.

Connecting to other services

These reach the internet, so each one only runs when you ask:

Connection How What is sent
Webhooks (Zapier, Make, n8n, IFTTT, your own) jot post <address> journal.jot, or Jot: Send to Webhook in VS Code (it asks first) the tasks, events and numbers as JSON: never the rest of your writing
Todoist jot todoist journal.jot with your API token in TODOIST_TOKEN, or Jot: Send Open Tasks to Todoist (the token is kept in VS Code's secret storage) each open task's text, due date and priority
Weather (Open-Meteo, no account) jot today journal.jot --weather 51.5,-0.12, or turn on jot.automation.weather.onToday with your location your latitude and longitude, rounded to about a kilometre

A webhook is the widest door: Zapier, Make and n8n turn it into thousands of services (a spreadsheet row per day, a message when a task is high priority, a note in another app). What arrives looks like this:

{ "format": "jot-automation", "version": 1, "file": "journal.jot",
  "tasks": [{ "text": "Post the letter", "status": "open", "priority": "normal", "date": "2026-10-28", "key": "…" }],
  "events": [{ "text": "Dentist 09:30", "date": "2026-10-28", "time": "09:30" }],
  "numbers": [{ "date": "2026-10-28", "metric": "steps", "value": 8200, "unit": "" }] }

Todoist gets each open task once. Jot remembers which tasks it has sent in a small record at the end of the journal (:::record sync #sync-todoist), so sending again only sends new ones. Formatted pages don't show this record.

The weather is written as a record, and its numbers chart like any others:

:::record observation #weather-2026-10-28
label: weather
sky: light rain
temperature-high: 14.3
temperature-low: 6.1
rain: 2.3
source: open-meteo.com
:::

Ideas

  • A scheduled job each morning (cron, Task Scheduler, a Shortcuts automation) running jot rollover and jot today, so the day starts with yesterday's open tasks waiting.
  • jot tasks journal.jot --status open --json in a Shortcut that shows your list on your phone's home screen.
  • A webhook to a Zapier zap that adds a spreadsheet row with each day's numbers.
  • Export on save to a calendar file your partner subscribes to, for shared plans.

Listening notes

In Write, choose Music & background media. Enter a song or episode title, artist, optional album and a share link from Spotify, YouTube Music or another service. Add a few words about the setting, then choose Add to this entry. The note is inserted at your writing cursor. It is ordinary Jot/Markdown that you can type or edit in any text editor:

#### Listening

“A small song” — An artist

[Open in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/track/example)

Captured: 2026-10-26T18:00:00.000Z

On the bus home. Rain against the windows.

Connect Spotify can fill in the title, artists, album and link for your account's currently playing track or episode. Press Fetch currently playing when you want a snapshot, review the fields, add your setting notes, and insert it. Fetching does not change the journal. Paused playback is labelled as paused. Playback is not polled in the background.

The manual option works without a connection. YouTube Music links can be entered manually; this website does not read another browser tab or Android's system media sessions. No microphone or media-file capture is part of this tool.

Music while you write

In Write → Music player ♫, paste a Spotify share link and choose Load Spotify player. Tracks, albums, playlists, artists, episodes and shows are supported. The player stays above the writing as you scroll and keeps the same music while you edit, switch preview tabs or enter focus mode. Choose music lets you replace it. Close player removes the embed and ends its playback; opening or closing the player never changes your journal.

Spotify is contacted only when you load a player. It may use cookies or ask you to sign in inside its player; playback and availability depend on Spotify, your account, browser and region. No Spotify developer app is needed for this embed, and Jot never receives the embed's account credentials. This is separate from the optional currently-playing capture connection below. If playback is unavailable, use Open in Spotify. Reloading the workspace does not reload music automatically. The player is excluded from journal downloads, page exports and print.

Spotify setup

Spotify requires a registered developer app. The site has no Client ID configured by default, so the connection needs this one-time setup before live Spotify capture can work:

  1. Open the Spotify developer dashboard and create or select a Web API app.
  2. In Jot's Music & background media → Spotify connection settings, copy the displayed redirect URL. Register that exact URL in the app. It ends in /write/spotify-callback.html. Production must use HTTPS. For local testing, open the site using 127.0.0.1 rather than localhost, and register its callback URL too.
  3. Copy the app's public Client ID into Jot. Do not enter a client secret. The public ID is remembered in this browser.
  4. Choose Connect Spotify, allow the sign-in window, and grant access to your currently playing information. Then fetch a song.

A site owner may set the public clientId in site/dist/jot/spotify-config.json instead, so visitors do not have to enter it. Spotify's current development-mode rules require a Premium app owner, allowlisted users, and a limit of five authenticated users. A public site deployment does not remove Spotify's app-access restrictions. See Spotify's quota modes for current requirements.

The connection uses Spotify's Authorization Code with PKCE and only the currently-playing permission. Access and refresh tokens stay in page memory and are never added to a journal, local storage or an export. Reloading the page ends the connection; Disconnect also clears it. You can revoke the app separately in your Spotify account settings. Existing notes stay readable and editable after disconnection. Your journal text is not sent to Spotify.

Scrobbling services

Listening → Last.fm / ListenBrainz can read a public profile's currently playing track or its ten most recent tracks. Choose the service, enter your username, and choose Fetch listening activity. Select a track to review, add your setting notes, then choose Add to this entry. Fetching only fills the fields; it does not change your writing or submit a scrobble.

  • ListenBrainz: public reads need a username, with no app registration or user token. Your player or scrobbler must already send listening activity to ListenBrainz. See its playing-now and recent-listens API.
  • Last.fm: enter your username and an application API key from Create an API account. Do not enter the shared secret. Public recent-track reads need no account authorization. See user.getRecentTracks. The key stays in this page's fields and is not saved.
  • Android: an optional app such as Pano Scrobbler can send supported players' activity to these services after you grant its permissions. Jot reads the service, not Android's notifications or media sessions.
  • Libre.fm: manual links remain supported. Direct fetching is not enabled: its public API returned an access challenge during integration checks, so browser access could not be verified. Follow its developer documentation for current API requirements; no unsupported proxy or account-password workaround is used.

A note labels the source and whether the service reported current playback or a recent listen. Available historical timestamps are stored separately as Listened, while Captured means when Jot fetched the details. “Playing now” is a service report, not a guarantee: players may send updates late or leave stale status. If nothing is reported, try recent tracks or enter the song manually. Editing the song fields clears the fetched provenance so it is not attached to a different song.

Only the requested username and, for Last.fm, application API key are sent to the selected service. The browser remembers a username after a successful fetch; no journal text is sent. There is no background polling, account write access or scrobble submission. Service errors leave existing writing and review fields unchanged. Requests are spaced and rate limits respected.

Albums, playlists and Spotify short links

An entry can hold any number of music references:

#### Music for this week

- Album: [An album to return to](spotify:album:4aawyAB9vmqN3uQ7FjRGTy)
- Playlist: [My writing mix](spotify:playlist:37i9dQZF1DXcBWIGoYBM5M)
- spotify: track:11dFghVXANMlKmJXsNCbNl

Copy a Spotify URI, or keep the type and ID from a share URL: https://open.spotify.com/album/ID becomes spotify:album:ID. The types are track, album, playlist, artist, episode and show. A space after spotify: is optional. Named Markdown links show your label; bare short references show “Spotify album”, “Spotify playlist”, and so on. Each becomes an ordinary link in the page preview and HTML export. Reading an entry does not contact Spotify or load music automatically. Paste the same short reference into Music player ♫ to load it for listening while you write. These are links to collections; the music itself is not copied into your journal or its .jotz package. You can always use a normal HTTPS link for other services.

In Music & background media → Songs, albums, playlists and more, paste one reference per line. An optional name goes before |, for example Writing mix | spotify:playlist:37i9dQZF1DXcBWIGoYBM5M. Add to this entry inserts the whole list at once; no title, account connection or now-playing fetch is required. You can mix Spotify references and HTTPS music links from other services. Review the list before adding; an invalid line is reported without inserting a partial note.

IMDb and YouTube background media

An entry can collect films, TV, episodes, videos and playlists alongside music:

#### Background media

- [Background film](imdb:tt0133093)
- [TV series](imdb:tt0386676)
- [Video](youtube:dQw4w9WgXcQ)
- [Video playlist](youtube:playlist:PL1234567890abcdef)

Use an actual provider ID from the link you want to save. IMDb uses imdb:tt… for title IDs (films, series and individual episodes). YouTube uses youtube:VIDEO_ID, optionally youtube:video:VIDEO_ID, or youtube:playlist:PLAYLIST_ID. A space after the first colon is optional. Bare shortcodes show a provider/type label; Markdown links give them a name. IMDb identifies the title and does not provide playback. These references do not fetch titles, ratings or thumbnails or embed videos automatically. The shared preview and HTML export expand them into ordinary HTTPS links.

In Music & background media, paste one reference per line, optionally Name | reference, and add the mixed list to the entry. Full IMDb title URLs and simple YouTube video/playlist URLs are shortened on insertion. Video links with timestamps or both a video and a playlist remain full URLs so their context is preserved. Existing journal writing is never automatically rewritten. The persistent writing player remains Spotify-only; YouTube references open YouTube when you follow them.

Find music IDs while typing

Open Music & background media → Find a song or album ID and enable Search MusicBrainz as I type. Choose song recording, album (release group), album edition, composition or artist, then type at least three characters in the dedicated search box. After a short pause, suggestions show names, artists and available dates, versions or durations. Choose a result with the mouse or Tab and Enter. It goes into the reference review list; Add to this entry is still needed to change the journal.

Only the search box text and chosen entity type are sent to MusicBrainz, with no account cookies or journal content. Search is off by default and turns off when the dialog closes. Requests are debounced/rate-limited, old searches are cancelled, and recent results are cached only for this page session. Busy/offline services show an error and leave manual entry available. Result names are not verified matches: check the recording/version or album edition before selecting one.

Database links use musicbrainz:recording:UUID, musicbrainz:release-group:UUID, musicbrainz:release:UUID, musicbrainz:work:UUID or musicbrainz:artist:UUID. They identify the music independently of Spotify or YouTube. Existing service links remain useful for playback; the lookup does not guess a corresponding playback URL. IMDb and YouTube remain manual links or shortcodes; their online search is not part of this MusicBrainz lookup.

Entry timezones and calendar export

Document Timezone: metadata supplies a default; @timezone: Europe/London inside a dated entry overrides it for that entry only. The next dated entry resets to the document default. Entry timezone in Write can add or remove an override. Entry dates and written clock times are preserved. Calendar export converts uniquely resolved timed events to UTC. Invalid declared zones, nonexistent times and repeated daylight-saving hours stop timed export instead of guessing. Use a complete RFC 3339 event start/at and, when supplied, end with explicit offsets to disambiguate. All-day dates stay dates. Multi-file CLI export keeps each file's timezone context independent. No declared zone means floating calendar times, not a device-zone assumption.

Insert current time is a separate explicit capture action, producing a full timestamp with its offset. Capture location uses Chromium's one-time geolocation permission and a review step; it neither tracks in the background nor infers timezone or address. See the writing guide for the source format and failure behavior.
